doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Teaching private sax, hearing loss, and his students
summary: He mostly teaches private saxophone to lower-level students after hearing loss from loud amps; he avoids putting anyone down.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Are we getting a lot of noise from that chair? Good. Okay. I’ll cut that part out. How have you seen the business change, of jazz education in the last ten or so years because of technology. The students that come to you, they’ve grown up in this everything is available on YouTube and on Spotify and so forth. Do you notice a difference in the students?

Well honestly the last ten years or so, I’ve been teaching mostly private saxophone. I’ve taught everything: jazz comp, arranging, all kinds of stuff. But some years ago I had found out more seriously that I had a hearing loss, probably from Blood, Sweat & Tears, from loud amp. So I got kind of panicky and said I don’t know if I can teach anymore. So I started teaching in the woodwind department, fifteen or twenty years ago. So I have my little room with a Yamaha upright piano and two people sit there and that’s it. Most of my students are not — I didn’t ask at the beginning when I was teaching there, but a lot of them are really, that’s not what they want to do is play saxophone. So I do the best I can but I don’t get emotionally tied to them one way or the other if they don’t come in prepared or whatever. You know, I don’t scream at students anyway, I’m just not like that. And if someone does great I say look, you listen to the teacher. I used to go home and tell my wife years ago teaching different classes, I said, “No one listens to the teacher.” I’m just being silly. New York silly. But most of my students are at a lower level. Level eight is the highest at Berklee whether you’re in ensembles or whatever. And I have like beginner improvisers, readers, some kids, they’ve been playing for ten years. I don’t tell them because I don’t want to hurt their feelings but they had a bad teacher in high school or junior high and they were like a band director. They didn’t play, they didn’t know about embouchure, they just gave them a horn, so they learned on their own a lot, and I don’t want to tell them, right, they’re like one year instead of ten years. So I have to start from the beginning. One good thing for me is my sax teacher, I’m kind of going off a little bit — like I say most of the students, they’re not high level, so there’s nothing really to compare yet because they haven’t been out there. I don’t listen very much to, I go on YouTube, I’ve almost stopped because I just want to take a break from that. I still listen to Sonny Stitt, my heroes, Bird and all the old jazz players and some

new people. Personally I’m at a point in my life I don’t really want to be putting anybody down. We all have opinions, what we like, just like foods or, why did I pick my wife? You know? That simple. But as some spiritual master said a while back, and I try to live these principles now, you know instead of bringing out the bad in someone, if you have something bad to say, bring out the good, even if they’re bad people. Because it’s going to bring out the better in you and it’s going to maybe open their hearts a little more and you might change that person. So that’s kind of a whole other trip.
